newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan lawmaker confidently mum on premier post.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan lawmaker confidently mum on premier post.

text.p: A heavyweight lawmaker widely tipped to become Taiwan's next premier denied any knowledge of such an appointment on Friday -- but spoke with the confidence of someone ready and willing to run a government.
"I very much appreciate everyone's concern about my future career," ruling Nationalist Party powerbroker Vincent Siew told Reuters in an interview.

"Until now, my superiors have not informed me about any change of my position. I really cannot comment on this at this moment," said Siew, who has been Taiwan's top policymaker toward rival China and its chief economic planner.

Government sources have told Reuters that the ruling party has settled on Siew as its choice to lead a new cabinet once Lien Chan, who was elected vice president in 1996, gives up the post to pursue his presidential ambitions.
Lien, under fire in recent months for a perceived breakdown of law and order, has said he would tender his resignation once key constitutional reforms are carried out in July.

Under Taiwan's evolving presidential-parliamentary hybrid, the elected president names a premier to run the cabinet as head of government. Parliament can veto a premier but is likely to lose this power in constitutional reforms now under debate.
The ruling party announced a modest cabinet shakeup in May in a bid to ease public anger, but bigger changes are brewing.
The ruling party's Central Daily News and other prominent media have said a new cabinet -- with Siew at the helm -- would be named at the Nationalists' August 23-27 party congress.
"Vincent Siew has solid political background and trust from high-level authorities," the Central Daily News said on Friday.

"He has background in mainland affairs, foreign policy, finance and economic matters as well as domestic affairs. He has the ability to plan and coordinate. Party high authorities have reached consensus about his appointment as premier."
A rising Nationalist star, Siew has represented President Lee Teng-hui at two Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summits and was handpicked by Lee to run for parliament seat in 1995.
Asked about his expectations for the new cabinet, Siew said the island's economy would top the agenda.
"Economic development and Taiwan are inseparable. It's the main bargaining chip for Taiwan's future survival," Siew said.

"We definitely want to maintain continued, stable economic growth. But we have to realise our people are concerned about other things -- quality of life, law and order, relations with the mainland, international recognition -- as well."
"The new cabinet should try its best to satisfy people's expectations," he said with a smile.
So familiar is that grin that local media have dubbed the 58-year-old politician "smiling old Siew".
Siew is generally seen as a relative liberal, in economics as well as politics.

Under his leadership, the cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council proposed to set up "offshore transshipment centres" -- an idea that in May allowed Taiwan and mainland ships to sail directly across the Taiwan strait for the first time since 1949.
Taiwan has banned direct links with the communist mainland since "generalissimo" Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist Republic of China lost a civil war 1949 and fled into exile on the island.
